clinicalPearls: Defined by the onset of progressive secondary sexual characteristics before the conventional age thresholds (around 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys), driven by premature reactivation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
Because it is gonadotropin-dependent, puberty progresses in the normal sequence and tempo, including testicular enlargement in boys and true breast development with a growth spurt in girls
A GnRH (LHRH) stimulation test showing a pubertal luteinising hormone response is the biochemical hallmark that distinguishes it from gonadotropin-independent (peripheral) causes
It is far more often idiopathic in girls, whereas an identifiable central nervous system lesion is more likely in boys and in very young children, mandating cranial imaging
Hypothalamic hamartoma is a classic structural cause and may be accompanied by gelastic (laughing) seizures
Bone age is advanced relative to chronological age, and untreated progression risks premature epiphyseal fusion and reduced adult height
First-line management is a long-acting GnRH analogue (agonist), which after initial stimulation down-regulates pituitary gonadotropin secretion and halts pubertal progression
reference.pathophysiology: Central precocious puberty results from premature reactivation of pulsatile hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion, which stimulates pituitary release of LH and FSH and consequent gonadal sex-steroid production. The activated axis reproduces normal puberty but at an inappropriately early age, so the sequence and progression of pubertal events are physiological. Triggers include disinhibition of the GnRH pulse generator by hypothalamic lesions (hamartoma, tumours, hydrocephalus, cranial irradiation, or previous chronic sex-steroid exposure), genetic changes affecting the pubertal timing network (such as MKRN3 loss of function), and, most commonly in girls, no identifiable cause. The premature sex-steroid exposure accelerates skeletal maturation, advancing bone age ahead of height gain.
additionalDifferentials: Gonadotropin-independent (peripheral) precocious puberty, including testotoxicosis and McCune-Albright syndrome
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia or a virilising/feminising adrenal tumour
Severe primary hypothyroidism causing overlapping pubertal signs
additionalInvestigations: GnRH (LHRH) stimulation test demonstrating a pubertal LH-predominant response
Basal LH and FSH with sex-steroid levels (oestradiol or testosterone)
Bone-age radiograph to assess skeletal advancement and height prediction
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and hypothalamic-pituitary region to identify a central lesion
Pelvic ultrasound in girls to assess uterine and ovarian maturation
Thyroid function tests to exclude profound hypothyroidism
redFlags: Neurological features (headache, visual disturbance, seizures, or gelastic episodes) suggesting an intracranial lesion
Precocious puberty in a boy or in a child under about 6 years, which carries a higher risk of underlying pathology
Very rapid pubertal progression with markedly advancing bone age threatening final height
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or new focal neurological deficit
reference.prognosis: Idiopathic central precocious puberty generally responds well to GnRH analogue therapy, with arrest of pubertal progression and preservation of adult height potential when treatment is started early; prognosis in secondary forms depends on the underlying central nervous system cause.
pitfalls: Relying on a single basal LH value, which may be prepubertal, rather than performing a stimulation test when suspicion is high
Omitting brain imaging in young children and in boys, in whom central lesions are more frequent
Confusing benign isolated premature thelarche or adrenarche with progressive true puberty
Delaying treatment until height potential is already lost
Overlooking a peripheral cause that has secondarily triggered central puberty
management: GnRH analogue therapy, such as depot leuprorelin, to suppress the reactivated hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and halt pubertal progression
MRI-directed treatment of any underlying central lesion such as hamartoma, tumour or hydrocephalus
Monitoring of pubertal signs, growth velocity and serial bone age to confirm efficacy and preserve adult height potential
Management of associated gelastic seizures where a hypothalamic hamartoma is present
Psychological and psychosocial support for the child and family
Timing cessation of analogue therapy at an age-appropriate point to allow normal resumption of puberty
